newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aussie dlr scared stiff as rate clock counts down.
newsitem.headline: Aussie dlr scared stiff as rate clock counts down.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished Friday on a soft note but again never threatened to escape the US$0.7470/7540 range which has dominated for a fortnight.

In a pattern that has become all too familiar, a short market tried to rally offshore only to recoil in the face of good European and NY bank offers. Traders reported exporter bids around US$0.7480 which cushioned the currency while the broader market waited to see if the Reserve Bank really would ease policy at next week's monthly board meeting.
There was more action on the crosses where rate changes saw the A$ sink on its Canadian cousin but rally against the NZ$.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar was loitering at US$0.7484/89 from an early US$0.7495/00 and US$0.7509/14 late here Thursday.

The currency has been caged in the US$0.7470/7540 range since sliding from atop 76 cents in the wake of shockingly weak May employment data released on June 11. The data were so bad it convinced the money market the RBA would soon be adding another 0.5 point cut to that made on May 23.
Some in the forex market had been playing down the risk but the median of analysts' expectations surveyed by Reuters still had it as a 50 percent chance after next week's board meeting.

The easing camp would have been reassured today by motor vehicle registrations data which showed a 0.7 percent fall in May when analysts had looked for a bounce of around 1.5 percent in a natural correction to April's hefty 6.1 percent drop.
The fall saw trend registrations turn lower for the first time since September last year and reinforced the impression the consumer had turned very cautious in the second quarter.
It also boded ill for the May retail trade data due next Wednesday where analysts were in the similar position of forecasting a bounce in sales following a shock 1.7 percent dive in April.

A soft result -- anything less than a 1.0 percent rise in sales -- would have the money market baying for an easing, assuming, that is, the RBA had not already moved at its 9.30 am policy window Wednesday morning.

The prospect contrasted with that in the U.S. where the Federal Reserve might just hike rates next week and with Canada which had already taken the plunge by tightening 0.25 point to 3.50 percent Thursday.
This was a seachange in Canadian policy, where rates had been cut no less than 11 times last year to a 36-year low, and a series of hikes was expected in the months ahead.

It was also significant for the A$ since it and the Canadian dollar tend to be seen as interchangeable by offshore investors. Both are part of the informal dollar bloc, both are commodity linked currencies and the economies are similar in many ways.
With domestic policy still in an easing phase, the interest differential between the two currencies was set to narrow sharply and put the A$ under pressure in the short term.

Key support is seen around C$1.0205, which marked a trough in February this year, a break of which would return the A$ to territory not visited since January 1996 and threaten a slide to parity and beyond.
The A$ had tumbled to C$1.0325/35 at the close from C$1.0484/95 ahead of the Canadian hike.

But analysts felt the prospect of further hikes would hurt the C$ bond market and could encourage portfolio switching out of Canadian bonds and into the better performing Australian bond market. This in turn would tend to support the A$ over time.
Elsewhere, the A$ was steady at 85.47/57 yen from 85.45/55 Thursday but off at 56.8 in trade weighted terms from 57.0.
On the Kiwi dollar the local currency climbed to NZ$1.0985/04 from NZ$1.0895/0911 after the RBNZ endorsed an easier policy in its six monthly Monetary Policy Statement.
The market actually went further than the bank asked for and took monetary conditions to 39 basis points below its target, partly in anticipation of a further official easing in Q4.

"In our view, the overall tenor of conditions and projections contained in the RBNZ's statement is consistent with lower NZ rates and, in particular, a lower NZ dollar over coming months," said Tim Moloney, an economist at CBA, summing up the sentiment of much of the market.
For the local market retail trade and building approvals data on Wednesday would be the next test assuming, of course, the RBA had not pre-empted them. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
